The final answer 138 is correct.

**Criterion.** Write $P(x)=\sum_j b_j (x)_j$ with $b_j\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then $p^k\mid P(m)$ for all integers $m$ if and only if $p^k\mid b_j\,j!$ for all $j$. The $x^n$-coefficient is $\sum_{j\ge n} b_j s(j,n)$. So a valid $P$ exists exactly when the ideal generated by $\{p^{e_j}s(j,n)\}$ contains 1, where $e_j=\max(0,\,k-v_p(j!))$. This holds if and only if some $j\ge n$ has $e_j=0$ and $p\nmid s(j,n)$, i.e. $k\le v_p(j!)$ and $p\nmid s(j,n)$. Hence
$$k(n,p)=\max\{v_p(j!): j\ge n,\ p\nmid s(j,n)\}.$$

**Locating the maximal $j$.** Using $(x)_{pm+r}\equiv (x^p-x)^m(x)_r \pmod p$:
- For $j=pn$, the $x^n$-coefficient is $[x^n](x^p-x)^n=(-1)^n\not\equiv 0\pmod p$.
- For $j=pn+r$ with $1\le r<p$, the factor $(x^p-x)^n$ has lowest term $x^n$, and $(x)_r$ has no constant term, so the $x^n$-coefficient vanishes mod $p$.
- For $j>pn+r$ with $m>n$, the factor $x^m$ forces every term to have degree $\ge m>n$, so again the coefficient vanishes mod $p$.

So the largest valid $j$ is $pn$, giving $k(n,p)=v_p((pn)!)=n+v_p(n!)$. The gcd condition for other primes is automatically satisfied, since $s(n,n)=1$.

**Sum.**
- $p=11$, $n=11,\dots,15$: $v_{11}(n!)=1$ each, so $k=12,13,14,15,16$. Sum $=70$.
- $p=13$: $k(11,13)=11$, $k(12,13)=12$, and $v_{13}(n!)=1$ for $n=13,14,15$ gives $k=14,15,16$. Sum $=68$.

Total $=70+68=138$.

VERDICT: ACCEPT
